Chronic

/KRAH-nik/ — stress on KRAH · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

A chronic problem or condition keeps going or coming back over a long stretch of time instead of going away quickly.

His chronic lateness meant friends told him events started thirty minutes early.

Worked Example

Her chronic back pain made every long flight miserable, though on good days she could forget about it entirely.

Chron (time) + -ic (having the characteristic of) = having the characteristic of time; lasting or recurring over a long period. The scenario shows a condition persisting over years, defining chronic. Key point: the pain is mild on some days but chronic regardless—the word is about duration, not severity.

How Chronic Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

persistent

persistent: continuing steadily without stopping

recurring

recurring: coming back again and again

ongoing

ongoing: still happening right now, not finished

Antonyms

acute

acute: in medicine, sudden and short-lived — an acute illness strikes fast and ends quickly, the opposite of a chronic one that lasts a long time

temporary

temporary: lasting only a short while, then gone

How Strong Is It? — occasional → recurring → persistent → chronic

occasional vs. chronic

occasional vs. chronic: An occasional headache shows up once in a while, but a chronic headache is part of nearly every day for months.

recurring vs. chronic

recurring vs. chronic: A recurring cough comes back a few times each winter, while a chronic cough never really goes away.

persistent vs. chronic

persistent vs. chronic: A persistent problem drags on for weeks despite your efforts, but a chronic condition can stretch on for years.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — chron

Root — chron: time — from Greek chronos (Greek)

Suffix — -ic

Suffix — -ic: characteristic of; having the nature of (Greek (via Latin -icus))

Put it together

Put it together: chron- (time) + -ic (characteristic of) = characteristic of, or lasting through, time. Anchor it to chronology, the time-order of events: a chronic problem stretches across the whole chronology of months or even years.

Use the root in a new word: synchronize

Use the root in a new word: synchronize: The swimmers practiced for weeks to synchronize their movements so both rose from the water at the exact same moment.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Use chronic when describing a problem, condition, or habit that persists or recurs over a long period. It emphasizes duration and repetition, not severity—a chronic condition can be mild. Avoid confusing it with intensity; it's about how long something lasts, not how bad it is.
